title: Models of Atonement
hook: Jesus died to save us from what: Satan, sin, or God's own wrath?
tldr: Christians have explained the cross in six major ways. For a thousand years the dominant answer was Ransom: Jesus freed us from Satan. Anselm's Satisfaction and then Calvin's Penal Substitution recast it as God punishing His Son in our place, and that model is where hellfire preaching really takes off.
big_idea: Your view of the cross shapes your view of hell.

points.title: Atonement decides everything about hell
points.text: Atonement, from "at one ment," is how humanity is reconciled with God. Your answer to why Jesus died is the foundation for all other doctrines, including the doctrine of hell.

points.title: For 1,000 years: Ransom from Satan
points.text: The earliest and most influential view, Christus Victor, says Christ's death freed humanity from Satan's bondage. Satan killed Jesus, not knowing sacrificial love would defeat him.

points.title: Love that changes hearts
points.text: Irenaeus saw Christ as a second Adam reliving and redeeming human life; Abelard saw the cross as a demonstration of God's love that turns sinners back to Him.

points.title: A feudal God's offended honor
points.text: Anselm, shaped by feudal Europe, saw sin as an affront to God's honor needing restitution. Christ's death satisfied that honor, a view that grew dominant in Catholicism.

points.title: Penal Substitution: God punishes the Son
points.text: Calvin built on Anselm: God poured His wrath, owed as eternal torture in hell, onto Jesus. This model is the greenhouse of the doctrine of hellfire as eternal conscious torment.

points.title: Twelve criticisms of PSA
points.text: It splits Father and Son, punishes the innocent, makes forgiveness require punishment, endorses violence, uses fear, and echoes pagan appeasement of wrathful gods.

points.title: Girard: the innocent scapegoat exposed
points.text: Girard's newer model sees Jesus as the ultimate innocent scapegoat, vindicated by resurrection, exposing society's violence and inviting forgiveness instead of revenge.

sections.h: How bizarre hellfire beliefs came to be
sections.summary: Before debating words and verses, it helps to understand the historical ideas beneath hellfire theology. Calvinist preacher Paul Washer, John MacArthur's protégé, claimed all creation will stand and applaud God as you enter hell because God has rid the earth of you. So much for "Love does not delight in evil" (1 Corinthians 13:6). Yet this accurately represents Augustinian-Calvinist theology, which rests on earlier doctrines, beginning with atonement.

sections.h: Why did Jesus have to die?
sections.summary: With hell, everything boils down to why Jesus died. The answer depends on whom you ask, where, and in what year. Atonement, originally "at one ment," is the bridge, adhesive, re-stitching and repair of humanity's bond with its Creator. Christian history offers six major theories of why Jesus died.

Irenaeus (130-202 AD) developed this view, held mostly by Orthodox churches. Christ lived every stage of human life, obeying where Adam disobeyed. Like David standing for Israel against Goliath, a patriarch for his family or a prime minister for his nation, Christ represents humanity. Adam's failure spread to all (Romans 5:12); in Christ all will be made alive (1 Corinthians 15:21-22).

Adam and Eve, in paradise with one rule, were deceived; Jesus kept the stringent Law of Moses flawlessly under the hardest circumstances and amid opposition. As our representative, He leaves Satan no claim over those who belong to Christ. He intercedes at God's right hand (Romans 8:34), is our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1) and lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25).

By far the most influential theory, and dominant for Christianity's first thousand years. Origen (185-254 AD) argued that after Adam's sin humanity was enslaved to Satan, "the prince of this world"; God offered Jesus as ransom, which Satan accepted, not realizing Jesus' divinity would defeat him. Gregory of Nyssa (335-394 AD) expanded it. Key ideas: enslavement to Satan, a ransom payment, and Christ the Victor breaking sin and death.

Jesus came "to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45) and "gave himself as a ransom for all people" (1 Timothy 2:5-6). By death He broke the power of the devil and freed those enslaved by fear of death (Hebrews 2:14-15). He canceled our legal debt, nailing it to the cross, disarming the powers and triumphing over them (Colossians 2:13-15).

sections.h: A cosmic battle and a kidnapped child
sections.summary: Jesus is a divine warrior defeating darkness by giving His life, echoing God freeing Israel from Pharaoh. Like a child lured by a stranger's candy despite warnings and kidnapped, humanity fell for Satan's deception; Jesus offers Himself as ransom. He came to drive out the ruler of this world, destroy the devil's works, plunder his house, end the thief's reign, and put all enemies under His feet.

The triumph is a "divine deception" or "cosmic sting operation." God used Satan's ignorance of sacrificial love and greedy lust for power against him: "None of the rulers of this age understood it, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8). Satan wanted to kill Christ, not knowing Christ came to die. Satan was overcome not by God's martial power but by His love.

In C.S. Lewis's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, the White Witch rules Narnia; Edmund conspires with her, and Aslan sacrifices himself in Edmund's place to defeat evil in the name of love. Calvinists criticize Lewis as "not an evangelical" with "significant deficiencies" on atonement, because he held Ransom. Atonement theology is the foundation for all other doctrines, including hell.

In Ransom theory Jesus took our place not so God could punish Him but so Satan could kill Him, a divine strategy defeating the devil through his ignorance of sacrificial love. That love, the spiritual "magic" evil did not know, is the ultimate power over evil, still true today. Ransom dominated until Anselm's Satisfaction theory challenged it in the late 11th century.

"Monkey see, monkey do": imitation is the cornerstone of learning, as infants copy parents, caregivers and even television, and adults copy others at work and socially. Hinted at by Church Fathers, it was systematized by Peter Abelard (1079-1142), who also held Ransom's substitutionary view (not Penal Substitution). Christ's death shared His creation's suffering, showing a love willing to die with and for it, a moral example to follow.

Sacrificial love provokes moral awakening, freeing sinners from selfishness. Mary Magdalene, saved from evil, imitated Christ's grace toward others. As kindness mends strained relationships, God's grace at the cross softens hearts. Abelard: Jesus died as a demonstration of God's love that can turn sinners back. God cannot cease to exist even a moment, so the death demonstrates love; and love works better than fear of punishment. "We love because He first loved us" (1 John 4:19).

Abelard offered Moral Influence as an alternative to Anselm's Satisfaction theory; Anselm rejected Ransom while Abelard sought to improve it. In Anselm and Calvin, Jesus reconciles a wrathful God; Abelard stressed that it is God "who through Jesus Christ reconciled us to Himself" (2 Corinthians 5:18). The synod in Sens, France excommunicated Abelard, yet his view lives on among non-conservative Protestants and some liberal Catholics and Orthodox.

Anselm of Canterbury (1033-1109), an Italian Benedictine monk, lived under feudalism, where knights could not forgive without punishment lest they look weak and invite revolt, and kings executed offenders to uphold honor. Influenced by Augustine and this culture, Anselm saw sin as an affront to God's honor that God could not forgive without restitution, with a penalty reaching the afterlife. His conception of God was significantly anthropomorphic.

Rejecting Ransom, Anselm said Christ's death restored, or satisfied, God's honor and retribution: God satisfying Himself, payment through retaliation for the debt owed His honor. Picture a king's son dying to save a subject condemned for offending the king. But the Father killing the Son sets God against Jesus, making the Son merciful and the Father cruel. Critics say it pictures a God unable to forgive without revenge. It became dominant in Catholicism.

John Calvin's 16th-century Reformation model built on Anselm: Christ redeemed humanity by taking God's punishment for sin, a punishment and abuse administered on Jesus by God. Substitutionary atonement (Christ suffers for us) differs from Penal Substitution (God punishes Christ in our place). Critics call PSA the most violent theory and a latecomer; defenders cite Eusebius of Caesarea (260-339 AD), but he said evil men, not God, made Christ suffer.

sections.h: In their own words: God killed Jesus
sections.summary: PSA is where hellfire preaching takes off. John MacArthur: "sin did not kill Jesus; God did." John Piper: Jesus "was bruised by his Father." Wyatt Graham of The Gospel Coalition: this "implies that God hates humans." Trevin Wax: "God killed Jesus." Mark Driscoll: "hatred for Jesus and love for us." C.J. Mahaney: "The Father killed the Son." David Platt: Jesus was "pulverized." A women's devotional: "God tortured His son."

"Penal" means penalty. Societies need consequences: under Moses' Law a thief repays more than he stole; today we pay speeding fines, and someone may pay another's fine. Calvin went further: God's justice demanded eternal torture in hell, and Jesus bore that full wrath. Ransom says Christ suffered for us; PSA says God punished Christ instead; Satisfaction repays lost honor, PSA pays a penalty that includes eternal conscious torment.

The Catholic church adopted Anselm's satisfaction theory and developed the idea of purgatory. The Protestant church upheld Calvin's Penal Substitution and continued to develop eternal conscious torment. Despite heavy criticism, PSA remains central in most Reformed, evangelical and conservative Protestant denominations, shaping their view of God's character, salvation and hellfire.

PSA is called the greenhouse of hellfire. Critics say it makes justice disproportionate and the relationship transactional. 1) It sets Father against Son, splitting the Godhead. 2) It punishes the innocent for the guilty. 3) It makes forgiveness require punishment, against Jesus' teaching. 4) It makes punishment the Gospel's essence, overshadowing love and resurrection. 5) It gives eternal punishment for temporal sins or lack of faith. 6) It mirrors patterns of trauma and abuse.

7) It makes violence necessary for salvation, against Jesus' nonviolence. 8) It puts retribution over mercy, risking legalism and cult-like community. 9) It is a modern development; Old Testament sacrifices were about purification, not punishment. 10) It is unfair to finite beings with limited knowledge. 11) It uses fear to motivate, though "there is no fear in love" (1 John 4:18). 12) A wrathful deity demanding an innocent victim is a pagan idea.

René Girard (1923-2015), French historian, critic and social philosopher, studied mimetic desire: we want things because others want them, which breeds rivalry. To avoid collapse, communities unconsciously blame a scapegoat; violence against it brings relief and becomes ritualized in myths, sometimes deifying the victim. The Gospels expose this: Jesus is the innocent victim, vindicated by resurrection and offering forgiveness, inviting us to break cycles of rivalry and revenge.

mythfact.myth: Christians have always believed God punished Jesus in our place.
mythfact.fact: For the first thousand years the dominant view was Ransom: Jesus freed us from Satan. Penal Substitution came with Calvin in the 16th century.

mythfact.myth: Substitutionary atonement and Penal Substitution are the same thing.
mythfact.fact: Substitutionary atonement means Christ suffers for us. Penal Substitution means God punishes Christ in our place.

mythfact.myth: Eusebius taught Penal Substitution in the early church.
mythfact.fact: Eusebius said Christ bore the curses due us, but evil men inflicted the suffering, not God.

mythfact.myth: Old Testament sacrifices were about punishing a victim.
mythfact.fact: They were about purification, not punishment; the New Testament likewise emphasizes reconciliation and restoration.

terms.meaning: From "at one ment": the means of reconciliation between humanity and God, repairing the bond with the Creator.
Irenaeus' view that Christ, a second Adam, relived human life obediently as our representative.
"Christ the Victor": the Ransom view that Jesus' death and resurrection defeated Satan and freed humanity.
Anselm's view that Christ's death restored God's offended honor and paid the debt owed to it.
Calvin's view that God punished Christ in our place with the wrath owed for sin.
Girard's idea that humans want things because they see others want them, leading to rivalry.

quotes.text: Jesus took our place, not so that God could punish him, but so that Satan could kill him.
Satan was overcome not by the martial power of God but by His love.
We must remember, however, that sin did not kill Jesus; God did.

verses.role: Love does not delight in evil, against the idea of creation applauding the damned.
In Adam all die, in Christ all made alive: basis of Recapitulation.
The Son of Man gave His life as a ransom for many.
Christ gave Himself as a ransom for all people.
By death Jesus broke the devil's power and freed slaves of the fear of death.
Debt nailed to the cross; powers disarmed and publicly shamed.
Rulers would not have crucified Christ had they understood: the divine sting.
We love because He first loved us: the heart of Moral Influence.
God reconciles us to Himself, rather than Jesus reconciling a wrathful God.
No fear in love, against PSA's fear-based motivation.

quiz.q: Which atonement model dominated Christianity's first thousand years?
quiz.why: Ransom, developed by Origen and others, dominated until Anselm challenged it in the late 11th century.

quiz.q: In Ransom theory, who killed Jesus?
options: Satan, unaware that sacrificial love would defeat him
No one; He did not die
quiz.why: Jesus took our place so Satan could kill Him, a divine strategy that defeated the devil through his ignorance of love.

quiz.q: What social system shaped Anselm's Satisfaction theory?
options: Feudalism, where lords could not forgive without punishment
quiz.why: In feudal Europe, knights and kings punished affronts to uphold honor; Anselm applied this to God's honor.

reflect: If your answer to why Jesus died changed, how would your picture of God's justice change?
